newsitem.title: USA: Bulgaria debt surges after assurances on payment.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria debt surges after assurances on payment.

text.p: Bulgaria's Brady bonds surged Tuesday after Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said the country would meet a $135.5 million coupon payment on its Brady bonds due January 28, emerging market experts said.
"The market really liked this," said Peter Allen, head of emerging markets research at BankBoston Corp. "If Bulgaria doesn't default, as I don't think it will, the spreads will tighten quite a lot."
At 1530 EST/2030 GMT, Bulgaria's IABs BGFLTH11=RR were 1-1/8 stronger at 51 bid.
Its FLRBs BGFLIRB=RR were 5/8 higher at 37-1/2 and the discount bonds BGFLTH24R=RR were 3/4 better at 55-3/4.

Based on Monday's closing prices, sources said the yield spread on Bulgaria's IABs narrowed nearly 100 basis points to around 1100 over U.S. Treasuries from 1200 over. Emerging market debt experts said another 200 basis point tightening is likely once a new government is in place and after a currency board system is implemented.
Bulgaria's Finance Minister Kostov announced Tuesday in Sofia that payment on the Bradies would be made through its State Fund for Reconstruction and Development (SFRD) which collects external loans.
"We could see the initial trade of 200 to 300 basis points (tightening) after the new government and after the currency board is in place," said one market strategist.
News that Bulgaria would be able to introduce a currency board by the end of February if the technical preparations are speeded up also helped boost prices.
"By the end of February we may be ready to introduce currency board rules if the technical preparations, which must be speeded up, are completed," Kostov told a news conference in Sofia on Tuesday.

Emerging market experts agree that the steps Bulgaria needs to take to emerge from its economic crisis will not be easy, but some believe the new government will implement the necessary policies to get the economy on track.
If the new government implements the right policies, one source said Bulgarian Brady instruments could provide investors with a hefty 30 to 40 percent return in 1997.

"There is a tremendous amount of mattress money in Bulgaria right now that should come back to the Central Bank and come back to the economy" after a currency board system is implemented, the source added. "It's going to be a difficult road but the Bulgarians have no choice.
